Tender
TEN-der
adj.
From Old French tendre, from Latin tener, soft, delicate, young. Webster 1828: soft; easily impressed or broken; susceptible of the softer passions; compassionate. In the Authorized Version tender describes three things — a young plant, a compassionate God, and a heart that can still be broken by His word.

Biblical Definition

Tender in Scripture is not weakness; it is the capacity to be affected. Its highest use belongs to God: David appeals to the multitude of thy tender mercies (Psalm 51:1) at the point where he has no other appeal left, and Zacharias names the whole incarnation as its fruit — Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us (Luke 1:78). The Hebrew and Greek behind these phrases are visceral words, drawn from the inward parts, and they mean compassion that is felt rather than merely decided. The word then describes what God commends in a man. Josiah is told, Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words (2 Chronicles 34:27) — the exact opposite of the hardened heart, and the reason the judgment was deferred in his days. Paul makes it the church’s manner: be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you (Ephesians 4:32), where the pattern and the power are both God’s prior forgiveness. And Isaiah uses the word of the Messiah’s beginnings: he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground (Isaiah 53:2) — unimpressive, easily despised, and the strength of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TENDER as soft; easily impressed, broken, bruised or injured; delicate; effeminate in constitution; also susceptible of the softer passions, as love, compassion, kindness; and careful not to injure.

expand to see more

TENDER, a. [Fr. tendre; L. tener.] — Soft; easily impressed, broken, bruised or injured; not firm or hard; as tender plants; tender flesh. Susceptible of the softer passions, as love, pity, kindness; compassionate. Careful to save inviolate, or not to injure; as tender of reputation. Young and weak.

Webster’s first sense — easily impressed — is the doctrinal one. A tender heart is one that takes an impression from the word of God, which is exactly what Josiah’s did and exactly what a hardened heart cannot do. The word is about receptivity before it is about sentiment.

Key Scripture

Luke 1:78 — "Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us,"

Psalm 51:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions."

2 Chronicles 34:27 — "Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, and humbledst thyself before me, and didst rend thy clothes, and weep before me; I have even heard thee also, saith the LORD."

Ephesians 4:32 — "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."

Isaiah 53:2 — "For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him."

Modern Corruption

Tender is corrupted when receptivity to God’s word is replaced by mere sensitivity to feeling — so that a tender heart comes to mean one easily upset rather than one easily convicted — and when God’s tender mercy is set against His justice as though the two were rivals.

expand to see more

The first corruption substitutes emotional delicacy for the thing Scripture praises. Josiah’s heart was tender in a specific and demonstrable way: he heard the words of the law, understood that judgment was deserved, humbled himself, rent his clothes, and wept — and then he tore down the high places. Tenderness there is the capacity to be broken by the word and to act on it. A man may be highly sensitive, quick to distress, and entirely unmoved by Scripture; that is not tenderness in the biblical sense but its counterfeit, and it can coexist with a completely hardened conscience. The test is not how readily a heart is affected, but by what.

The second corruption sets God’s tenderness against His justice, so that tender mercy becomes an argument for expecting God to overlook sin, and eventually for denying that He will judge at all. But Psalm 51 is prayed by an adulterer and murderer who has just been confronted by a prophet, and it appeals to tender mercies precisely for the blotting out of transgressions — the mercy is aimed at guilt, not at its dismissal. Luke 1:78 locates that tender mercy in the visit of the dayspring from on high, which is to say in the incarnation of the One who would bear the judgment. Tenderness and justice meet at the cross rather than competing, and a tenderness that costs God nothing is not the tenderness the Bible describes.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two word families supply tender. One is the language of the womb and the inward parts, used of God’s compassion; the other is the plain adjective for what is soft, young, and easily impressed, used of plants and of hearts.

expand to see more

Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — compassion, tender mercies; a plural noun built on the word for womb (Psalm 51:1).

Hebrew rācham (H7355) — to have compassion, to show deep mercy; the verb of the same family.

Greek splagchnon (G4698) — the inward parts, and by metonymy the seat of compassion; behind the tender mercy of our God (Luke 1:78).

Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft, weak, gentle; used of Josiah’s heart (2 Chronicles 34:27) and of the tender plant of Isaiah 53:2. Greek eusplagchnos (G2155) is the New Testament’s tenderhearted (Ephesians 4:32).

Usage

"The multitude of thy tender mercies (Psalm 51:1) is what a guilty man appeals to when he has nothing else."

"Josiah’s heart was tender (2 Chronicles 34:27) — he heard the word, humbled himself, wept, and then acted."

"The Messiah grows as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground (Isaiah 53:2): unimpressive, and the arm of the LORD."
